lessons.title: Lesson 1: What consultants do and where AI fits
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain what a consultant does and three ways AI helps them.
This lesson builds toward: Given examples of consulting work, you will explain what a consultant does and three ways AI helps them, naming at least two client problems that match your military skills.
A consultant is an outside expert a client hires for a specific job, for a set time. Examples: setting up a safety program for a construction company, building a training plan for a nonprofit's volunteers, or planning a warehouse layout.
AI helps consultants research a topic fast, draft documents like proposals and reports, and turn notes into checklists or slides. It does not replace your experience: clients pay for your judgment.
AI consulting also includes helping small organizations start using AI tools safely, for example writing a simple AI-use policy or training staff. Your military habits of standard procedures and clear training translate well.
Words to know:
- Consultant: an outside expert paid to solve a specific problem for a client.
- Client: the person or organization that pays for your service.
- Deliverable: the thing you hand over at the end, such as a plan, report or training.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "What problems do small businesses near me often hire consultants for?" Circle two that match what you did in the military.
You can now explain what a consultant does and how AI supports the work.

options: What you hand over at the end, like a plan or report
check.why: A deliverable is the finished work the client receives.

check.q: AI gives you a list of problems small businesses hire consultants for. What do you do?
options: Offer to fix all of them
Circle the ones that match what you did in the military
Pick the one that pays most, even if you have no skill in it
check.why: Your offer should match real problems with the skills you already have.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Turning your expertise into an offer
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-sentence offer: who you help, the problem, and the result.
This lesson builds toward: Using your military expertise, you will write a one-sentence offer that names who you help, the problem and the result, tested by asking at least one person in that field.
A clear offer has three parts: who you help, what problem you fix, and what result they get. For example: "I help small construction firms build a written safety program so they pass inspections and cut injuries."
Start with what you did often and well in service, then find civilian groups with the same problem. A former logistics NCO might help small distributors plan inventory. A former trainer might help nonprofits onboard volunteers.
Use an AI assistant to brainstorm, then test the offer by asking two or three real people in that field: "Is this a problem you would pay to fix?"
Step by step:
- List three things you did often and well in service.
- Ask an AI assistant: "Which civilian businesses have this problem?"
- Write: "I help [who] [fix what] so they [result]."
- Ask two or three people in that field if they would pay for it.
Words to know:
- Offer: a clear statement of who you help, with what, and the result.
- Niche: a small, specific group of clients you focus on.
Try it now: Write your one-sentence offer using "I help [who] [fix what] so they [result]." Ask an AI assistant to make it clearer, then read it to one person in that field.
You can now write a clear consulting offer based on your military expertise.

options: A small, specific group of clients you focus on
check.why: A niche is the specific group you serve, which makes your offer clear.

check.q: You wrote "I help businesses with stuff." What do you do?
options: Rewrite it as "I help [who] [fix what] so they [result]"
Make it longer with more buzzwords
check.why: A clear offer names who you help, the problem and the result.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Free official help for veteran business owners
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find the free veteran business help near you and know what each office does.
This lesson builds toward: When you plan your business, you will identify the free official veteran business help near you and what each office does, with the nearest Veterans Business Outreach Center's contact and one question to ask.
The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) runs Boots to Business, part of the military Transition Assistance Program, and Boots to Business Reboot for veterans of all eras. Veterans Business Outreach Centers (VBOCs) offer business plan workshops, mentoring and training.
If you want government contracts, the SBA certifies veteran-owned and service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses through its Veteran Small Business Certification program, called VetCert, at certifications.sba.gov. When we checked in October 2026, VA said businesses that work with VA must be registered through SBA.
VA also lists entrepreneurship training as a way to use some GI Bill benefits. Business names, licenses and taxes are set by your state and the IRS, so check your state's business office and irs.gov, or ask a VBOC advisor.
Step by step:
- Open the SBA veteran-owned businesses page.
- Find your nearest Veterans Business Outreach Center.
- Look at Boots to Business or Reboot dates.
- If you want government work, read about VetCert at certifications.sba.gov.
- Check your state business office for licenses and registration.
Words to know:
- SBA: U.S. Small Business Administration, the federal agency that helps small businesses.
- VBOC: Veterans Business Outreach Center: SBA-funded centers that help veteran business owners.
- VetCert: SBA's certification for veteran-owned and service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses.
Official sources:
- SBA: Veteran-owned businesses
- SBA: Veteran contracting assistance (VetCert)
- VA: Veteran-owned small business support
- VA: How to use your GI Bill benefits
Try it now: Find the Veterans Business Outreach Center nearest you on sba.gov. Write down its name, how to contact it, and one question you will ask about starting a consulting business.
You can now find free official help for starting a veteran-owned consulting business.

check.q: What does a Veterans Business Outreach Center offer?
options: Free business plan help and mentoring for veterans
check.why: VBOCs give veterans free business planning help and mentoring.

check.q: You have a question about the business license you need. Where do you take it?
options: Your state business office, irs.gov or a VBOC advisor
check.why: License and tax questions go to official offices or advisors, not the AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing your first outreach message
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short, honest message that asks a possible client for a 15-minute call.
This lesson builds toward: For your offer, you will write a short, honest outreach message that asks a possible client for a 15-minute call, with every claim true and three people to send it to.
Your first clients often come from people who already know you: former leaders, veteran groups, local business groups and nonprofits you volunteer with.
A good outreach message is short: who you are, the problem you help with, one proof (a result from service or past work), and a small ask, such as a 15-minute call.
AI can draft it, but make it sound like you and remove anything that is not true. Never claim a certification, clearance or result you do not have.
Step by step:
- List ten people or groups who know you or share your field.
- Ask an AI assistant for a 5-sentence message: who you are, the problem, one proof, a 15-minute call.
- Edit it to sound like you.
- Check every claim is true.
- Send it to three people.
Words to know:
- Outreach: contacting possible clients to start a conversation.
- Proof: a real result that shows you can do the work.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to draft a five-sentence outreach message for your offer. Edit it so it sounds like you and every claim is true, then write the names of three people you will send it to.
You can now write an honest outreach message that asks a possible client for a short call.

check.q: What is a good small ask in an outreach message?
check.why: A small, easy ask like a short call makes a first yes more likely.

check.q: The AI's outreach draft says you have "20 years of consulting experience". You have none. What do you do?
options: Remove it and state your real military experience
check.why: Every claim must be true; your real experience is your proof.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Writing a proposal with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Draft a one-page proposal with AI and edit it until it is accurate.
This lesson builds toward: Given your offer and a client's problem, you will draft a one-page proposal with AI and edit it until it is accurate, with a clear scope, a timeline and a price you set yourself.
A proposal is your plan for the client's problem. It works like an operations order: situation (the problem), mission (what you will do), execution (steps and timeline), and what the client gets (deliverables).
Give the AI your notes from the client call, with no private client data, and ask for a one-page proposal using those headings. Then edit hard: cut anything vague, fix dates, and make the scope clear so the work does not keep growing.
You set the price, not the AI. Think about your hours, your costs and what the result is worth to the client. Ask a VBOC advisor or other consultants in your field what is normal.
Step by step:
- Write your notes from the client conversation (no private data).
- Ask an AI assistant for a one-page proposal: problem, what I will do, timeline, deliverables, price.
- Make the scope specific: what is in and what is not.
- Add your own price.
- Read it as the client: is anything unclear?
Words to know:
- Proposal: a written plan and price for solving a client's problem.
- Scope: exactly what work is included and what is not.
- Scope creep: when a job keeps growing beyond what was agreed.
Try it now: Use your offer and a made-up client. Ask an AI assistant for a one-page proposal with the five headings, then edit the scope and add your own price.
You can now draft and edit a clear one-page consulting proposal with AI help.

check.q: What does scope mean in a proposal?
options: Exactly what work is included and what is not
check.why: Scope sets clear limits on the work, which prevents scope creep.

check.q: The AI suggests a price for your proposal. What do you do?
options: Set your own price based on your hours, costs and value
Ask the client to pick any price
check.why: You set the price; the AI does not know your costs or value.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Delivering the work and protecting the client
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set rules for using AI on client work that protect the client's information.
This lesson builds toward: When you use AI on client work, you will write rules that protect the client's information and check AI work before delivering it, with an AI-use line in the proposal and no client data in public tools without permission.
Clients trust you with their information: staff names, money, plans and problems. Do not paste a client's private or confidential information into a public AI tool unless the client has agreed and the tool is approved for it.
Check every AI output before the client sees it: facts, numbers, names and laws. You are responsible for the work, not the AI.
Be open about how you use AI. A simple line in your proposal works: "I use AI tools to draft documents; I review all work and do not share your private information with them."
Step by step:
- Keep client private data out of public AI tools.
- Use placeholders like [client name] when drafting.
- Check every fact, number and law before delivery.
- Add one line to your proposal about how you use AI.
Words to know:
- Confidential: information the client wants kept private.
- Approved tool: an AI tool the client has agreed you may use with their information.
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page proposal. Add your AI-use line, check every claim is true, and write the name of the free official business office you will contact next.
You can now offer consulting based on your military expertise, write a proposal with AI, and protect your client's information.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Problem and offer The client's problem or what you will do is vague. States the client's problem and what you will do, matching your offer. Uses the client's own words for the problem. Scope, deliverables and timeline No clear scope, deliverables or timeline. Clear scope (what is and is not included), what the client gets and a timeline. Says how changes to the scope will be handled. Your price No price, or the AI's price used as is. A price set by the learner. The learner can explain the price from hours, costs and value. Client information protected No AI-use line, or client details pasted into a public AI. A clear line on how AI is used and how client information is protected. Placeholders were used in all AI drafting. True claims and next step A claim is not true, or no office named. Every claim is true, and one free official business office is listed as the next contact. The learner has a question ready for that office. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does a placeholder like [client name] do?
options: Lets you draft with AI without sharing private details
check.why: Placeholders keep client details out of the AI while you draft.

check.q: A client sends confidential plans and you want AI help. What do you do first?
options: Paste them into any public AI
Check the client agreed and the tool is approved for it
check.why: Confidential client information goes into an AI tool only with the client's agreement and an approved tool.
